title: Mid-II Revision & Papers
scope: Revision: functions and recursion (Unit III), structures/pointers (Unit IV), and preprocessor/files (Unit V). Historical papers retain their printed scope; this is not a prediction of current exam coverage.

parameters.title: Actual and formal parameters
paragraphs: Actual arguments are expressions supplied in a call: sum(a,b). Formal parameters are local objects declared by the definition: int sum(int x,int y). The values of a and b initialize x and y. Names need not match, but argument types/order must match the prototype.
Changing x alone does not change a. Passing &a instead copies its address into a pointer parameter, through which *p can change a.

modular.title: Functions and modular programming
paragraphs: A function is a named block that performs a defined task. Modularization divides a larger problem into cohesive functions with clear inputs, outputs and responsibilities.

Advantages include reuse, reduced duplication, readable structure, isolated testing/debugging and easier maintenance. A function call can have overhead; meaningful decomposition matters more than splitting every statement.

syntax.title: Function syntax
paragraphs: Definition: return_type function_name(parameter_list) { declarations_and_statements; return expression; }. A non-void function returns a compatible value; a void function returns no value and may use return; or reach its closing brace.

Example: int sum(int x,int y) { return x+y; }. Declaration before use: int sum(int,int);. Call: int total=sum(5,3);. Here int is the return type, sum the identifier, x/y formal parameters and the braces contain the body. Use (void) for no parameters in a C 11 prototype.

value.title: Value and address arguments
paragraphs: C passes every argument by value. Integer parameters are copies; changing them leaves the caller’s integers unchanged. The classroom term call by reference means passing addresses into pointer parameters and updating pointed-to objects.

For the example below, value_swap exchanges local 3 and 7 but caller remains 3,7. address_swap receives copies of &a,&b; dereferencing them changes caller objects to 7,3. Valid live objects are required.

scope.title: Local/global variables and lifetime
paragraphs: A block-local variable is visible from its declaration to the end of its block, including nested blocks unless shadowed. A file-scope variable is visible from its declaration through the translation unit; external linkage can permit references from other translation units.

Scope describes where a name is usable; storage duration describes how long an object exists. Automatic local objects normally last for a block execution; static-duration objects last for the entire execution. A local static variable retains its value between calls while its name stays block-local.
Example: int g=1; void f(void) { int local=2; static int calls; ++calls; }. g is file-scope; local and calls are block-scope; calls has static duration.

storage.title: Storage classes
paragraphs: In the introductory classification: auto is the usual automatic block-local object; register is a request for fast access for an automatic object (no address-of on that register object); static gives static storage duration and, at file scope, internal linkage; extern declares an object/function with linkage, commonly defined elsewhere.

Do not equate lifetime with scope. A block-local static object has program-long duration, and a file-scope extern declaration need not be the definition. A variable’s address does not reveal whether it is auto/static; no fixed address output is promised.

recursion.title: Recursion and its characteristics
paragraphs: Recursion occurs when a function calls itself directly or indirectly. A valid terminating algorithm needs a base case and progress toward it; each active invocation has its own parameter/local state.

It naturally expresses recursive definitions and divide-and-conquer problems. Costs include call overhead, stack use and possible repeated work or stack exhaustion. The factorial example reduces n until 0, then combines products while calls return.
recursion.basis_label: Priyanka class notes, supplemented by senior notes

libraries.title: Library and user-defined functions
paragraphs: Library functions are provided by the implementation/library, with declarations in standard headers: printf in stdio.h, strlen in string.h, malloc in stdlib.h, sqrt in math.h. Headers declare interfaces; functions execute when called.

User-defined functions are written for the application, such as int sum(int a,int b). Both need compatible declarations and valid arguments. Source strrev/strupr/strlwr are extensions, not ISO C 11 string functions.

ackermann.title: Ackermann function
paragraphs: For nonnegative integers: A(0,n)=n+1; A(m,0)=A(m−1,1) for m>0; A(m,n)=A(m−1,A(m,n−1)) otherwise.

Pseudocode: if m=0 return n+1; else if n=0 return A(m−1,1); else return A(m−1,A(m,n−1)). This is nested recursion: the inner result becomes the outer call’s second argument. Growth is very rapid; a practical demonstration must tightly bound inputs.

recursion-iteration.title: Recursion versus iteration
paragraphs: Control: recursion repeats through function calls; iteration repeats through loop conditions and updates. Termination: recursion reaches a base case; a loop makes its continuation condition false or exits explicitly.

State: recursive activations preserve separate call state; iterative solutions normally maintain explicit variables (or an explicit stack when needed). Resource use: ordinary recursion consumes call-stack space and call overhead; an equivalent simple loop can use constant extra space.
Clarity depends on the problem: tree traversal often reads naturally recursively, while summing a flat array is usually simpler iteratively. Neither method is universally faster or safer.

categories.title: Four function interfaces
paragraphs: The four combinations are: arguments with returned value; arguments without returned value; no arguments without returned value; no arguments with returned value. Every function has a return type—without return value means void, not an omitted type.

The example defines four separately named functions. The first returns the addition result to main; the second prints it inside the helper; the third reads and prints internally; the fourth reads internally and returns for main to print. C has no function overloading by signature.

factorial.title: Recursive factorial
paragraphs: Initialize the mathematical definition with 0!=1. For n>0, n!=n×(n−1)!. Each call reduces n, and the base value returns through the pending multiplications.
For 5: fact(5)=5×fact(4)=5×4×3×2×1×fact(0)=120. Reject negative input and bound the result type before allowing the computation.
factorial.basis_label: Priyanka class notes, supplemented by senior notes

recursive-set.title: Factorial, GCD, Ackermann and Fibonacci
paragraphs: These are four separate recursive tasks, not one recurrence. Factorial uses 0!=1 and n×fact(n−1); GCD uses gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,a%b), ending at b=0; Fibonacci uses two base cases; Ackermann nests recursive calls.
The source repeats Factorial in its slash-separated list; it is represented once here. Each program below has its own input contract and example trace; compile/run them separately.
recursive-set.basis_label: Priyanka class notes, supplemented by senior notes; GCD supplied by general PPS knowledge (note gap)

array-pass.title: Pass arrays to functions
paragraphs: Passing a[i] supplies one scalar element value. Passing a in an ordinary function call converts the array expression to a pointer to its first element; an int a[] parameter is adjusted to int*. It does not copy a whole array or carry its length.

Pass the valid length separately. Use const int a[] for a helper that only reads elements; use int a[] when element changes are intended. sizeof on an adjusted parameter does not recover the original array capacity.

matrix.title: 2D-array parameters and matrix multiplication
paragraphs: A 2 D array is an array of rows. A parameter int a[][2] adjusts to a pointer to a two-int row, retaining the column extent for indexing. It is not int**. For arbitrary dimensions, use a correctly declared dimension-aware interface.

For A with r×k and B with k×c, multiplication requires equal inner dimensions and C has r×c entries. Reset each C[i][j] to 0, then sum A[i][t]×B[t][j] for t=0..k−1. The program demonstrates fixed 2×2 values and shows all four dot products.

bubble.title: Bubble sort using a function
paragraphs: Pass the array pointer and valid size. Scan adjacent pairs across the unsorted prefix, swapping only when the left value is larger. After each pass the largest remaining value reaches its final position.

Shrink the next pass by one; j<n−i−1 keeps j+1 valid. Mutation through the array pointer persists in the caller. This fixed-pass version is quadratic even for already sorted data; an early-exit flag would be a separately identified optimization.

structure.title: Structures, tags and member access
paragraphs: A structure groups named members into one aggregate type; members may have the same or different types. Example: struct student { int roll; char name[20]; int marks[3]; }; defines a tagged type, then struct student s; declares an object.

The tag student identifies the type for further declarations and self-referential pointer members; it does not allocate an object by itself. Use s.roll, s.marks[0], and p->roll for a valid struct student* p=&s. The arrow expression equals (*p).roll.

union.title: Structures versus unions
paragraphs: A structure gives distinct storage to its members, so all member values can coexist. A union overlays member storage: writing one member changes the stored representation shared by the others. Track which member was last written.

Both can group named members and use dot/arrow access. Structure and union sizes can include alignment padding; sizeof(struct) need not equal the member-size sum, and sizeof(union) need not equal exactly the largest member size.

Unions support alternative representations in tagged records (for example integer or floating readings) and memory-saving storage when alternatives are not needed simultaneously. Use a separate tag to remember the active alternative.

array-structure.title: Arrays and structures
paragraphs: An array stores a sequence of elements of one element type and selects them with indices: marks[i]. A structure stores named members selected with dot/arrow: student.roll. Member types need not all differ.

An array of structures is a sequence of complete records, such as struct student class[5]. An array within a structure is a member such as int marks[3]; each student has its own marks array. This models multiple students and their multiple subject marks together.

nested.title: Nested structures
paragraphs: A nested structure has a structure-typed member inside another structure. This models grouped information, such as a student containing an address.
Access follows each member: s.home.city. The example initializes roll/name/address, then prints them; the enclosing student and nested address remain separate types.

students.title: Array of student records with totals and percentage
paragraphs: An array of structures keeps the same fields for each student. Read each student’s roll,name,address and three marks, reset total for that student, add the marks, then calculate percentage using floating division.

The supplied bank specifies 5 students and 3 subjects. For this solution each subject is assumed out of 100, so percentage=total/300×100. If the maxima differ, use their actual sum instead. Name/address input is bounded to single tokens in the example.

self.title: Self-referential structures
paragraphs: A self-referential structure contains a pointer to its own tagged type, for example struct node { int data; struct node *next; };. It can link another node, itself or NULL; it does not automatically point to itself.

This supports linked lists, trees and graphs. A direct member of the same incomplete structure type is invalid because its size is not yet complete; a pointer member is permitted. NULL is a macro for a null pointer constant, not a C keyword; test before dereferencing.

pointer.title: Pointers and their uses
paragraphs: A pointer object holds a pointer value designating an object/function, a null pointer, or a permitted one-past array position. Example: int x=7; int *p=&x; then *p accesses x. Initialize before use and respect type, lifetime and array bounds.

Uses include caller-object updates through address arguments, array/string traversal, dynamically allocated storage and linked data structures. In int *p,q only p is a pointer. Print an object pointer with %p and (void*)p, not %d or %u.

pointer-array.title: Pointer arithmetic and pointers to arrays
paragraphs: For int a[3], int *p=a points to its first element, while int (*row)[3]=&a points to the entire row array. An array of pointers is different: const char *names[3] stores three pointer objects.

Pointer plus/minus an integer and ++/-- move by element units, scaled by sizeof the pointed-to type. Same-array subtraction counts elements and yields ptrdiff_t. Stay in the same array or one-past; never dereference one-past. Unrelated-object subtraction, pointer multiplication/division, void* arithmetic and function-pointer arithmetic are not ISO C.
p+1 computes a new pointer without updating p; p++ updates p. Neither increments *p. Array expression conversion to &a[0] in context does not make a assignable.

array-pointers.title: Array of pointers
paragraphs: An array of pointers stores pointer elements, for example const char *names[3]={"Asha","Bina","Chitra"};. names[i] selects a pointer; names[i][j] selects a character of its pointed-to string.
This differs from char names[3][20], which stores three fixed-size character rows, and from a pointer to an entire array. String literals are not modifiable; use const char*.

pointer-string.title: Pointers to strings
paragraphs: A char pointer can traverse a terminated character sequence; stop before the null character and never pass the buffer boundary. Literals should be accessed through const char* when not modifying them.

An array of string pointers holds separate pointers and may refer to strings of different lengths; a pointer to a character array instead retains its row extent. The example shows string traversal followed by all entries of a pointer array.

function-pointer.title: Pointer to a function
paragraphs: Declaration: int (*operation)(int,int);. Parentheses make operation a pointer to a function taking two int parameters and returning int. Without them int *operation(int,int) declares a function returning int*.

Example: int add(int a,int b) { return a+b; } then int (*operation)(int,int)=add; and int result=operation(2,3); gives 5. Function pointers support callbacks/selected operations; function-pointer arithmetic is invalid.

dma.title: Dynamic memory allocation
paragraphs: Dynamic allocation obtains storage during execution, useful when size/lifetime is not known as a fixed automatic array. Include stdlib.h and check size calculations and allocation results.

malloc(n*sizeof *p) allocates uninitialized bytes; calloc(n,sizeof *p) allocates zeroed bytes; realloc(p,new_size) resizes, possibly moving storage; free(p) releases it. Free(NULL) is harmless. Do not assume zero bytes represent a null pointer or every floating representation.

For nonzero new size use a temporary for realloc, so failure leaves the old allocation available. Initialize added elements and free successful allocations on all paths. Avoid zero-size resizing in beginner code because its semantics are version/implementation-sensitive.

struct-pass.title: Passing structures to functions
paragraphs: Pass a structure value to make a copy; pass a pointer to read/update the original through ->; pass selected members if the helper only needs those values. Returning a structure value is permitted.

There is no universally best method. Value parameters isolate changes and are natural for small records. A const pointer avoids copying a large read-only record; a writable pointer is appropriate when changing caller fields. All pointer arguments are still passed by value.

pointer-invalid.title: Four-dimensional indexing and unrelated-pointer subtraction
paragraphs: (i) For a genuine four-dimensional array a, a[i][j][k][l] is equivalent to *(*(*(*(a+i)+j)+k)+l). Each dereference selects the next array level; every index must be valid.

(ii) The printed program subtracts p=&a and q=&b for two separate scalar objects. They are not elements of the same array, so p−q has undefined behavior. There is no portable numerical output, even if addresses appear adjacent on one run.

For a valid comparison example use one array: int v[2]; ptrdiff_t distance=&v[1]-&v[0]; gives 1, printed with %td. The source expression is retained for analysis rather than silently changed into a valid program.

file.title: Files and text/binary streams
paragraphs: A file is a named external data resource accessed through a stream. FILE *fp is a pointer to the C library’s stream-control object, declared in stdio.h; it is not itself a byte-position counter. fopen returns a stream pointer or NULL.

Text streams represent text and can translate newline representations. Binary streams transfer bytes without that text translation. Text numbers need parsing/formatting; native binary numeric/structure representations are implementation-dependent. Neither kind is inherently encrypted.

modes.title: Opening files and modes
paragraphs: Syntax: FILE *fp=fopen("data.txt","r"); if(fp==NULL) handle failure; then close with fclose(fp) and check failure. r reads an existing file; w writes and truncates or creates; a appends and creates if needed.

Adding + permits both reading and writing: r+ does not truncate; w+ truncates/creates; a+ permits reading and appending, with writes forced to the current end regardless of positioning. Add b for binary mode, such as rb or wb. Initial read position in append mode can vary; position explicitly if needed.
For update streams, respect read/write transition rules: output to input requires fflush or positioning; input to output requires positioning unless input encountered EOF. Do not use fflush(stdin).

seek.title: Random-access file positioning
paragraphs: fseek(fp,offset,origin) sets position relative to SEEK_SET (start), SEEK_CUR (current), or SEEK_END (end), returning 0 on success. ftell(fp) returns a position indicator as long or−1 L on failure. rewind(fp) returns to start and clears error/EOF indicators; it has no return value.

On a binary stream where supported: fseek(fp,15 L,SEEK_SET) requests 15 bytes from start; fseek(fp,-5 L,SEEK_END) requests 5 bytes before end. The latter fails if unsupported or inappropriate for the file—always check the result.

Text streams restrict portable fseek offsets: zero, or a previous ftell value used with SEEK_SET. Do not promise arbitrary byte-relative seeks on text files. Sequential access processes data in order; random access explicitly repositions to a chosen location.

formatted-file.title: Formatted and character file I/O
paragraphs: fprintf(fp,"%d\n",value) formats a value into a stream; fscanf(fp,"%d",&value) parses it, returning the number of assigned conversions. Check that result before using value. fprintf returns a negative value on output failure.

fgetc/fputc read/write one character; fgets reads a bounded line including a newline if it fits; fputs writes a terminated string without adding a newline. Keep fgetc result as int until EOF is distinguished. Close the stream and check errors.

binary.title: Binary file I/O
paragraphs: fwrite(ptr,size,count,fp) writes count objects of size bytes; fread(ptr,size,count,fp) reads them. Both return completed item counts, not bytes unless size=1. Use rb/wb modes and verify the count.

The example writes a record, closes, reopens, reads exactly one record and prints its fields. Raw struct files are not portable across arbitrary compilers/architectures due to representation and padding; define explicit serialization for interchange.

errors.title: File error handling
paragraphs: Check fopen against NULL, input functions against their success criteria, output functions for errors and fclose for failure. After a failed read, ferror distinguishes an error from ordinary end-of-file.

feof reports an end indicator after a read reaches past the end; while(!feof(fp)) is not a correct read loop. clearerr resets both indicators. perror writes a message using errno; use it immediately after the failing operation.

command.title: Command-line arguments
paragraphs: A conventional hosted entry is int main(int argc,char *argv[]). argc is a nonnegative argument count; when argc>0 argv[0] represents the program name if available, argv[1] is the first supplied argument, and argv[argc] is NULL.

Check the count before indexing. Arguments are strings; numeric conversion needs validation (for example strtol with end/range checks). Quote text containing spaces so the shell passes it as one argument. The example prints one argument and its length.

enum-typedef.title: enum and typedef
paragraphs: enum declares an enumerated type and named integer constants: enum day { MON, TUE, WED };. With no explicit values these are 0,1,2. Explicit initializers can choose different values; subsequent uninitialized enumerators increment from the previous one.

typedef introduces a type alias: typedef unsigned long count_t; count_t total=0;. It does not allocate storage or create a distinct new type. For a tagged record: typedef struct student { int roll; } Student; permits Student s; as an alias spelling.

preprocessor.title: Preprocessor directives and symbolic constants
paragraphs: Directives begin with # and act during preprocessing. #include <stdio.h> includes a standard header; #define LIMIT 10 defines an object-like symbolic constant; #define SQUARE(x) ((x)*(x)) defines a function-like macro.

#undef removes a macro; #if/#ifdef/#ifndef/#elif/#else/#endif select conditional compilation; #error produces a diagnostic; #pragma requests implementation-specific behavior. A directive is not an ordinary runtime statement and does not generally end in a semicolon.

Macros substitute tokens, not typed function calls. Parenthesize arguments/results and avoid repeated evaluation of side-effecting arguments; an inline function is often preferable for such operations.

file-count.title: Write/read and classify file characters
paragraphs: Write a known sequence, close successfully, reopen for reading and inspect each successfully read character. Count all characters; digit and special-symbol counts are subsets, not additional characters.
The program states exactly which characters are written and defines special as neither alphanumeric nor whitespace. Use unsigned-char values with ctype classification and distinguish EOF using int.

copy.title: Copy one file and display the copy
paragraphs: Open the input before opening the output; reject open failures. Read until fgetc returns EOF and write each returned character. Check read, write and close results before claiming success.

The example copies a fixed fixture input.txt to copy.txt in binary mode, then reopens and displays the copy. Different destination name avoids truncating the input; a general filename-taking solution should reject the same underlying file.

even-odd.title: Separate even and odd numbers into files
paragraphs: Read each successfully parsed integer; n%2==0 identifies even values and the remaining integers are odd, including negative odd values. Write each to its corresponding output stream and check all results.
The demonstration first writes 1,2,3,4 to a text file, then produces even.txt containing 2,4 and odd.txt containing 1,3. The fixed fixture makes the otherwise unspecified input data reproducible.

inventory.title: Inventory file example
paragraphs: The prompt does not specify an inventory schema. This authored interpretation uses item ID, single-token name, quantity and unit price. Write one text record, read it back and calculate stock value=quantity×unit price.

For a production inventory, validate fields and record format, preserve existing records when updating, and handle invalid/missing files. The example is deliberately a small standalone illustration, not an unspecified full inventory application.

macro-output.title: Macro expansion trace
paragraphs: The paper defines sqr(x) as (x*x), without parentheses around each parameter. Thus sqr(a+b) expands to (a+b*a+b), not ((a+b)*(a+b)).

For a=5,b=6, multiplication happens first:5+6×5+6=41. A corrected macro #define sqr(x) ((x)*(x)) would give 121 for the same side-effect-free argument. Keep the printed macro when answering the output question; changing it would change the question.

pointer-sort.title: Sort through a pointer to an array
paragraphs: Declare a pointer to the entire array with int (*row)[5] and pass &a. Inside the helper, *row provides the first-element pointer for the adjacent comparisons. This retains the five-element array extent, unlike int* or int**.

Apply shrinking bubble-sort passes to the selected row. The first pass gives 12,1,4,9,20; the second gives 1,4,9,12,20; further fixed passes leave it unchanged. Use strict greater-than comparisons to preserve equal-element order.

array-within.title: Array within a structure
paragraphs: An array within a structure is a member such as int marks[3]; each structure object owns its own complete marks array. This differs from struct student class[5], an array of whole student records.
Access a subject with s.marks[j] or p->marks[j] for a valid pointer p. In the example below, the three-subject marks array is a member of each of five student structures.

swap.title: Value copies and pointer swap
swap.note: Local parameters are copies. The pointer helper exchanges the two pointed-to objects; pointer arguments themselves are still passed by value.

categories.title: Four argument/return combinations
categories.note: Distinct function names demonstrate the four interfaces in one program. The first pair use caller-supplied operands; the second pair read internally. Demonstration inputs are limited to ±1000 to keep int addition representable.

factorial.title: Recursive factorial
factorial.note: Base case0!=1. For5: fact(5)=5×4×3×2×1×1=120. Limit0..20 keeps all products within the minimum required unsigned long long range; recursion depth is bounded.

fibonacci.title: Recursive first n Fibonacci terms
fibonacci.note: F0=0,F1=1 and Fn=F(n−1)+F(n−2). Six terms end at F5. Naive recursion repeats calls; count0..20 is a teaching/runtime bound, not a universal Fibonacci limit.

gcd.title: Recursive Euclidean GCD
gcd.note: For nonnegative inputs, gcd(48,18)→gcd(18,12)→gcd(12,6)→gcd(6,0)=6. Both-zero input is rejected; input contract is nonnegative integers at most one million.

ackermann.title: Bounded Ackermann demonstration
ackermann.note: A(0,n)=n+1; A(m,0)=A(m−1,1); otherwise A(m,n)=A(m−1,A(m,n−1)). A(2,2)=7. Only m≤3,n≤6 accepted because nested recursion grows rapidly; not an unrestricted evaluator.

array-sum.title: Pass an array and its length
array-sum.note: The array argument converts to a pointer; const prevents element changes through this parameter. Pass n separately. Each value is within ±1000 and capacity is20; the long sum is then representable.

matrix.title: Pass 2D arrays and multiply matrices
matrix.note: A fixed2×2 worked example: c00=1×5+2×7=19,c01=1×6+2×8=22,c10=3×5+4×7=43,c11=3×6+4×8=50. The parameter retains column extent2; arbitrary dimensions are not claimed.

bubble.title: Bubble sort through an array parameter
bubble.note: Pass1:12,1,4,9,20; pass2:1,4,9,12,20; pass3 and4 unchanged. The fixed-pass version performs n(n−1)/2 comparisons, so best/worst time is quadratic; strict adjacent swapping is stable and uses constant extra space.

students.title: Five student records with three marks
students.expected:
1 A X total=210 percentage=70.00
2 B Y total=150 percentage=50.00
3 C Z total=300 percentage=100.00
4 D W total=0 percentage=0.00
5 E V total=180 percentage=60.00
students.note: Source asks for5 students and3 subject marks. Authored assumption: every subject is out of100; percentage=total/300×100=total/3. Names/addresses are single whitespace-delimited tokens here; full lines require bounded line input.

nested.title: Nested student/address structure
nested.note: home is a structure member; s.home.city selects a nested member. The sample data and address fields are authored to illustrate the source’s unspecified nested-student example.

union.title: Union active-member example
union.note: The members share storage. Read count while it holds the stored integer, then read price after writing it; do not expect both values preserved. Structure/union sizes can include padding, so do not equate sizeof with a raw sum or largest-member size.

self-reference.title: Two self-referential nodes
self-reference.note: A same-type pointer links objects; it need not point to the same object. Traversal stops at NULL before dereference. Stack objects remain alive throughout main; allocation and deletion are separate topics.

dma.title: malloc, calloc, realloc and free
dma.note: malloc gives uninitialized storage; calloc zeroes allocated bytes (giving integer zeros here). realloc can move storage; retain old pointer on failure by using tmp. Initialize the newly added element. Free each successful allocation exactly once; never use freed pointers.

pointer-array.title: Pointer arithmetic and pointer to an array
pointer-array.note: p+1 advances one int; int (*row)[3] points to the entire three-element array. The same-array difference counts elements and has ptrdiff_t type (%td). One-past may be formed but not dereferenced; no multiplication/division of pointers.

struct-function.title: Structure value, pointer and scalar members
struct-function.note: Value parameter copies a structure; member arguments pass selected scalar values; pointer parameter can mutate the original object. For large read-only structures prefer const struct student* when appropriate; no method is universally best.

pointer-string.title: String and array of string pointers
pointer-string.note: A pointer to a string is distinct from an array of pointers. Literals are not modified; const char* expresses that restriction. Each pointed-to sequence ends in a null character.

copy-file.title: Copy and display a file
copy-file.note: Fixture input.txt contains Hello C followed by newline. rb/wb copy bytes without text translation. fgetc result is int to distinguish EOF; detect input/write/close failures. The copied file is reopened and displayed.

file-count.title: Write a file, then count character classes
file-count.note: Writes A1 ! followed by newline (five characters). All characters count; digit count is1; special means neither alphanumeric nor whitespace, so only ! counts. Cast to unsigned char for ctype classification.

file-errors.title: Detect and clear stream error indicators
file-errors.expected:
EOF=1 error=0
After clearerr: EOF=0 error=0
file-errors.note: Read using the function result rather than while(!feof). feof is set only after a read attempts past the end. ferror distinguishes a read error; clearerr resets both indicators. perror reports the errno-associated message when an operation fails.

binary.title: Write and read a binary record
binary.note: fwrite/fread transfer one object-sized record and return item counts. This native-layout file is for the same implementation; raw struct padding, integer/float representation and endianness make it unsuitable as a portable interchange format.

command-line.title: Print arguments and length of a supplied string
command-line.note: Run as program hello; quote an argument containing spaces. argc counts program-name entry plus supplied arguments when present, argv[argc] is a null pointer. Check argc before accessing argv[1]. strlen returns size_t (%zu).

macro.title: Object-like and function-like macros
macro.note: The preprocessor expands SQUARE(a+b) to ((a+b)*(a+b))=49. Parentheses protect precedence, but the argument is evaluated twice: do not pass i++ or other side effects. #include includes headers; #if/#ifdef control conditional inclusion.

even-odd-files.title: Write integers and split into even/odd files
even-odd-files.note: numbers.txt contains1,2,3,4; even.txt becomes2 and4, odd.txt1 and3, one value per line. Uses a fixed small fixture to illustrate the source’s unspecified integer-data example; detect malformed input and stream failures.

inventory.title: Inventory record in a text file
inventory.note: Inventory fields are an authored interpretation: ID,name,quantity,unit price. Store a text record, reopen/read it and compute stock value3×12.50=37.50. The source gives no required inventory format.

pointer-sort.title: Sort through a pointer to an array
pointer-sort.note: int (*row)[5] receives &a, the address of the entire five-int array; *row converts to the first-element pointer for adjacent swaps. Fixed capacity5 retains the row extent. Pass1:12,1,4,9,20; pass2:1,4,9,12,20; remaining passes unchanged.

paragraphs: On a binary stream where supported, request position15 bytes from the start. Check fseek returns0; otherwise positioning failed.
